a8.speaker: European Commission (EU executive)
a8.speech: "In order to ensure the timely availability and supply of defense products from the European Defense Technological and Industrial Base and to accelerate its adjustment to structural changes, thereby strengthening the efficiency of the financial assistance granted, it is important to establish minimum conditions related to the value generated within the Union. Therefore, common public contracts must provide for the obligation that the costs of components originating in the Union, the States of the European Economic Area [EEA] or Ukraine must not be less than 65% of the estimated costs of the final product." ; further states that "the cost of components originating in the Union, [...] the EEA or Ukraine cannot be less than 65% of the estimated cost of the final product." ; "no component may come from another third country that runs counter to the security and defense interests of the Union or its Member States." ; calls for strengthening the single market for defense products and services in the EU and cooperation on public contracts in the security area (a minimum of 35%), and, whenever possible, the use of European preference ; wants harmonized and simpler rules, more support for Ukraine, pan-European projects, collaborative partnerships within the EU and cooperation outside the EU, such as with Canada, the United States, Norway, the United Kingdom, Turkey, India and the Indo-Pacific ; asks EU member states to activate the national escape clause by April and quickly adopt the regulation on strengthening European armament and manufacturing, as part of an 800 billion euro plan for EU defense ; asks that the next long-term EU budget provide for a comprehensive and solid framework to support EU defense.

a48.speaker: Information Minister of The Gambia (unnamed)
a48.speech: Said his ministry is committed to building the website of all other ministries, a strategic move to enhance relations with the media and chart a way forward for the government to communicate to the public.

a48.speaker: Yankuba Saidy, Deputy Permanent Secretary, Gambia Information Ministry
a48.speech: Said the government is working to ensure media outlets are subvented so they can sustain their operations.

a48.speaker: Imam Alhagie Muhammed Lamin Touray, former President of The Gambia's Supreme Islamic Council
a48.speech: In his sermon, preached peace, unity and stability, and urged Muslims to fulfil their religious obligations with dedication. Expressed profound gratitude to President Barrow for sponsoring the mosque's construction, recalled past struggles to raise funds, and said: "This singular act will enhance the spiritual development of the community." Thanked women, youth, and religious leaders for their support.

a48.speaker: Chief Falalo Touray and Alkalo Dembo Darboe of Gunjur
a48.speech: Commended the President, noting that the mosque, together with ongoing road and infrastructure projects, will promote the religious and social development of Gunjur, and urged residents to support the President to enable him to continue his development agenda.

a48.speaker: Hamat N.K. Bah, Minister of Regional Government, Lands and Religious Affairs
a48.speech: Described the Gunjur mosque as one of the most modern in the country, built to meet contemporary architectural standards. Disclosed that President Barrow has funded several mosque projects nationwide, reflecting his commitment to Islam. Echoed calls for Gambians to support the President's re-election bid in December, and thanked elders and religious leaders for preaching peace and tolerance.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: At the Gunjur mosque inauguration: thanked the Gunjur community for the honour, described Gunjur as a historic Islamic settlement, thanked anonymous donors who funded the mosque, and urged the community to pray for them. Challenged residents to take good care of the mosque, and pledged government support for its upkeep. On the December elections, said: "There are no losers in elections... A peaceful and credible process promotes The Gambia's image as a democratic country."

a48.speaker: Saikou Dukureh, Gambian Consul General in Gabon
a48.speech: Welcomed the President and thanked him for the engagement; described Gambians in Gabon as hardworking, united, and law-abiding, and commended the government for supporting their welfare.

a48.speaker: Jakarta Dampha, Gambian community representative in Gabon
a48.speech: Said there has been marked improvement in the well-being of Gambians in Gabon since President Barrow took office, and that the President's leadership has ensured Gambians in the diaspora are not discriminated against.

a48.speaker: Hawa Dukureh, Gambian youth representative in Gabon
a48.speech: Commended the President for dispatching a team of immigration officials to issue national documents; said nearly 200 people were processed, but appealed for support to ensure the passports are delivered.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: At the Gabon diaspora meeting: expressed gratitude for the warm reception; said dialogue is key to national unity; reaffirmed his government's commitment to assisting Gambians abroad and said the decision to send immigration officials to Gabon was to ensure citizens have access to documents; pledged to prioritise delivery of processed passports. Updated the community on domestic progress (roads, electricity, health, transport, education), and encouraged those with voter cards to exercise their right to vote.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: Aboard the ferry launching his nationwide development tour: said the tour reflects his government's strategy of delivering social projects directly to ordinary Gambians, and said: "Infrastructure is the foundation upon which all other sectors rely," describing it as a key pillar of his development agenda.

a48.speaker: Unnamed resident (Fass Njaga Choi)
a48.speech: "This road has been our dream for years. We thank the President for remembering us,"

a48.speaker: Alhaji Kala Darboe, resident (Bakalar)
a48.speech: Said the new Hakalang feeder road will create opportunities for women and farmers, while improving access to education, healthcare, and other essential services.

a48.speaker: Dr Ahmadou Lamin Samateh, Gambia Minister of Health
a48.speech: Described the new Buduk health post as "another significant milestone", reflecting the government's commitment to improving healthcare services.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: On the Buduk health post: said the opening aligns with his administration's broader goal of ensuring access to quality healthcare for all Gambians.

a48.speaker: Lamin Saidykhan, North Bank Region Governor
a48.speech: Commended the government for what he described as unprecedented development that has transformed livelihoods in the area, and urged residents to reflect on the impact of these projects on ordinary people.

a48.speaker: National Assembly Member for Badibou (unnamed)
a48.speech: Described the Njaba Kunda gathering as significant, attributing continued support for the President to the government's track record of delivering roads and health centres where previous administrations had failed.

a48.speaker: Alhaji Jagne, Chief of Central Badibou, and Councillor Maimuna Bah
a48.speech: Expressed gratitude to the President, recalled past difficulties accessing health facilities due to poor roads, and said patients can now reach care within minutes thanks to the new road, health centre, and ambulances.

a48.speaker: Fatou Kinteh, Gambia Minister of Gender and Children's Welfare
a48.speech: Said President Barrow's development agenda is visible across all sectors, particularly in women's empowerment, noting women now hold influential government positions, and called on women to support the President.

a48.speaker: Sulayman Sumareh, Managing Director, National Roads Authority
a48.speech: Disclosed that the Salikenni–Njaba Kunda road is fully government-funded, and said the project will improve connectivity and enhance access to health, education, and other social services.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: At the Salikenni–Njaba Kunda road inauguration: described the new road as part of his government's plan to connect all communities, saying "The North Bank Region has received unprecedented attention under this government with the construction of several roads." Reassured citizens of his administration's commitment to infrastructure and urged communities to maintain the projects.

a48.speaker: Kebba Jallow, former leader of the People's Progressive Party (PPP)
a48.speech: Reaffirmed his support for President Barrow, saying the President has done so much for the country and deserves another term in office.

a48.speaker: Seedy S.K. Njie, Deputy Public Relations Officer, National People's Party (NPP)
a48.speech: Welcomed the PPP executives into the Alliance, and said President Barrow is pleased to accept the endorsement.

a48.speaker: Gibril Faal, CEO, GK Partners
a48.speech: Briefed the President on GK Partners' activities, particularly its Diaspora Fellowship project with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), and updated him on progress in diaspora direct investment, noting The Gambia now leads in monitoring remittance data through the Central Bank of The Gambia.

a48.speaker: Adama Barrow, President of The Gambia
a48.speech: On meeting with GK Partners: underscored his commitment to supporting the project and urged GK Partners to do more public relations work to inform Gambians about their initiatives.

a161.speaker: SNCF (French state-owned rail company, statement and social media post)
a161.speech: Says its high-speed network has been targeted by "malicious acts" aimed at paralysing the system: "Last night, the SNCF was victim of several acts of vandalism on the Atlantic, Northern and Eastern high-speed lines. Fires were deliberately set to damage our installations." ; Warned that the situation could last "at least all weekend while repairs are conducted". ; Advised rail passengers who can postpone their trip to do so and "not to go to the station", noting only the Atlantique, Nord and Est TGV lines are impacted and that tickets for disrupted journeys are exchangeable and refundable: "Following this massive attack aimed at paralyzing the high-speed line network, a large number of trains were diverted or cancelled."

a161.speaker: Patrice Vergriete, French Transport Minister (social media post)
a161.speech: "Co-ordinated malicious acts targeted several TGV lines last night and will seriously disrupt traffic until this weekend. I strongly condemn these criminal actions which will compromise the vacation departures of many French people." ; Went on to thank SNCF staff for trying to restore services "as quickly as possible".

a161.speaker: Source close to the investigation (anonymous), via AFP news agency
a161.speech: Says the arson attacks were acts of "sabotage" and added that the attacks were "evidently co-ordinated".

a174.speaker: Nhlanhla Nene, South African Finance Minister
a174.speech: During his medium-term budget policy statement last year, Nene warned that an additional R22 billion needs to be found; he has prepared the public and investors for the possibility of raising the necessary revenue through tax increases.

a174.speaker: National Treasury
a174.speech: The Treasury has said an extra R44 billion must be raised over three years.

a174.speaker: Democratic Alliance (DA, alternative budget speech)
a174.speech: In its alternative budget speech on Tuesday, the DA said "a tax increase is both an unnecessary and unjustifiable burden on everyday South Africans".

a174.speaker: Democratic Alliance (DA, alternative budget)
a174.speech: The party said cutting corruption and maladministration could save R10 billion; they want the National Youth Development Agency and SETAs scrapped, claiming savings of R11 billion, and reducing the size of Cabinet by getting rid of deputy ministers, said to save R335 million. ; The DA said it could cut the public sector wage bill by R4.3 billion through avoiding raises higher than inflation, cutting spending from certain departments and linking salaries to performance. ; The DA wants Eskom's dominance on power supply broken up and divided into separate generation and transmission units allowing independent power producers into the market to raise competition.

a174.speaker: Cosatu
a174.speech: Cosatu has called for a host of new taxes, including a new category for the super-rich, a tax on luxury items and on exports of strategic minerals.

a174.speaker: Cosatu
a174.speech: "The current energy crisis which [Zuma's] plan prioritises cannot be an excuse for the privatisation of state owned assets," said Cosatu Tuesday. "We expect the minister to provide more resources to Eskom to enable it to execute its developmental mandate appropriately. The effectiveness of Eskom cannot be measured by the extent to which its balance sheet becomes more profitable but rather by the extent to which it can provide energy security to the country."

a174.speaker: Public sector unions
a174.speech: The offer of inflation-linked pay rises has been declined and the public sector unions have demanded a one-year deal with a 15 percent increase.

a174.speaker: Iraj Abedian, CEO of Pan-African Capital Holdings
a174.speech: Told Business Day on Tuesday that if the state failed to keep increases in the wage bill and social grants below inflation it would lead to sovereign credit downgrades.

a174.speaker: Nhlanhla Nene, South African Finance Minister
a174.speech: Last year, Nene said state assets would be sold to help cover the injection of cash Eskom needs to keep functioning.

a174.speaker: Cosatu and the United Front
a174.speech: Are calling on the minister to move away from what they see as a trend of austerity budgets and embrace a pro-poor plan introducing new measures to boost the economy and combat poverty, unemployment and inequality.

a320.speaker: Dr. Kalumbi Shangula, Namibian Minister of Health and Social Services
a320.speech: While handing over the boat, noted the important milestone the donation marks in the ministry's mission to provide integrated, affordable and quality health care services responsive to public needs: “It addresses a specific challenge of maritime transport. The Ministry of Health and Social Services remains steadfast in its dedication to ensuring that all citizens, irrespective of their location, have access to necessary healthcare services. This boat is a testament to that commitment.”

a320.speaker: Bernard Sisamu, Kabbe North constituency councillor
a320.speech: Applauded the gesture, noting how timely the donation is and the challenges it will address with the ongoing flash floods and yearly transport difficulties in flood-prone areas: “This occasion could not have come at a more appropriate time than this, as we have already witnessed in Namibia and other countries the negative effect from rain, which is causing flooding.”

a389.speaker: AFP reporter at the court
a389.speech: Said former DRC leader Joseph Kabila went on trial in absentia Friday on charges including treason over alleged support for Rwanda-backed militants.

a389.speaker: Charge sheet (DRC military court)
a389.speech: Said Kabila also faces charges including homicide, torture and rape linked to the anti-government force M23, as well as 'taking part in an insurrection movement', 'crime against the peace and safety of humanity' and 'forcible occupation of the city of Goma' ; described Kabila as 'one of the initiators of the Congo River Alliance' (AFC), the M23's political arm, accused him of colluding with Rwanda to try to 'overthrow by force the power established by law', and accused him of being responsible for atrocities committed by the movement in the North and South Kivu provinces.

a389.speaker: Felix Tshisekedi, President of the DRC
a389.speech: Has branded Kabila the brains behind the armed group, which has seized swathes of the resource-rich Congolese east with Rwanda's help.

a389.speaker: Emmanuel Shadari, Secretary General of Kabila's People's Party for Reconstruction and Democracy (PPRD)
a389.speech: Dismissed the trial as a 'political trial' that he said would 'divide the Congolese people' during peace negotiations: the proceeding 'is anything but a fair trial. With a justice system that is not independent, the conviction is already decided - the rest is theatre, a ridiculous staging.'

a389.speaker: Samuel Mbemba, Deputy Justice Minister
a389.speech: Told reporters at the hearing: "The courts do not negotiate, they will do their work independently."

a389.speaker: Rwanda (government)
a389.speech: Denies providing military backing to the M23.

a389.speaker: UN experts
a389.speech: Say Rwanda's army played a 'critical' role in the M23's offensive in the region.

a389.speaker: Benjamin Mbonimpa, executive secretary of the AFC and M23
a389.speech: Distanced the movement from Kabila at a news conference in Goma, saying the government should not 'label him an AFC/M23 member' just because he had come to the city; Kabila 'as a Congolese citizen is free to go wherever he likes', branding the trial part of a 'malevolent strategy' against the ex-president.

a389.speaker: Joseph Kabila, former President of the DRC
a389.speech: Has branded his successor's government a 'dictatorship'.

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Warned, in an interview with Christiane Amanpour on CNN, of the serious economic consequences of the new US trade policy for Africa, stressing that "47 of the 54 African countries would be directly affected," leading to a "potential decline in export revenues and foreign exchange reserves" ; "when these currencies weaken, two things will happen: first, most of these countries, being import-dependent, will face high inflation; second, the cost of servicing debt denominated in local currency but contracted in foreign currency will increase."

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Insisted on the importance of avoiding a trade confrontation with Washington: "Africa cannot afford a trade war with the United States," recalling that the continent represents only "1.2% of American world trade, about 34 billion dollars, with a surplus of 7.2 billion."

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Proposed a three-pronged strategic response: "flexible and constructive trade negotiations with the United States; a diversification of export markets; and the acceleration of the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)."

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Rejected the idea of an exclusive realignment of Africa towards China, declaring that "the United States is a key ally of Africa, just like China. Africa builds bridges, it does not isolate itself" ; recalled the continent's desire to build "balanced, transparent and mutually beneficial partnerships" with all its partners, including the European Union and the Gulf states.

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Denounced the paradigm of aid dependency, affirming that "the era of aid as we have known it is over," and argued for "bold investments in domestic resource mobilisation, infrastructure and value-added industrialisation."

a418.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB) Group
a418.speech: Stressed that the AfDB had already invested more than 55 billion dollars in infrastructure and that its "High 5" flagship initiatives had reached more than 565 million people; highlighted "Mission 300," a joint initiative with the World Bank to connect 300 million people to electricity by 2030: "Without electricity, what can one do? It is impossible to industrialise, to create added value, to be competitive in the dark."

a421.speaker: Shamsa Warsan, mother of a malnourished child in Baidoa
a421.speech: "They told me my child is malnourished."

a421.speaker: Somalia's federal government and the UN (new data)
a421.speech: New data warns that worsening drought, conflict, and soaring food prices could push 4.4 million people — nearly 23 per cent of the population — into hunger this year.

a421.speaker: World Food Programme
a421.speech: Says children under five will be among the hardest hit, with around 1.7 million expected to suffer acute malnutrition by December 2025.

a421.speaker: Aid agencies on the ground
a421.speech: Say US funding cuts have deepened the crisis, forcing some life-saving clinics to shut their doors.

a421.speaker: Binyam Gebru, deputy country director for Save the Children in Somalia
a421.speech: "Nobody saw this coming. We have had to lay off around 150 people because of funding, we have to close field offices and it has compromised our capacity to deliver." ; "If we do not have the resources we cannot provide those very low cost but high impact interventions, children will die."

a421.speaker: Stand Up For Aid, grassroots advocacy group (figures)
a421.speech: According to its figures, the US has slashed $170 million in aid to Somalia.

a421.speaker: Abdullahi Isak Ganay, Vice Minister for Humanitarian and Disaster Management in South West Somalia
a421.speech: Issued an even starker warning: "If the aid is cut during this crisis, we could end up in a situation like we did in 1991."

a421.speaker: Al Shabaab
a421.speech: Claiming to have seized a military base and the town of Wargaadhi.

a421.speaker: Somali government
a421.speech: Denied Al Shabaab's claim to have seized a military base and the town of Wargaadhi.

a421.speaker: Binyam Gebru, deputy country director for Save the Children in Somalia
a421.speech: On Al Shabaab's advance: "This is a very dangerous turning point." ; "That will impede our capacity to deliver supplies to communities."

a421.speaker: Hodan Abdi Warsame, displaced woman in Baydhabo camps
a421.speech: "I used to live in Deygaab village. After my husband passed away, I didn't receive any help. I had to flee due to hunger, and eventually, I arrived here in Baidoa seeking assistance." ; "Since then, I was forced off my farm. Al Shabaab got involved in the matter, but nothing was ever resolved. Now, I am here alone, while my children are still back in the village." ; "Al Shabaab told me they want someone who would take care of the children. They said they wouldn't hand over the children to a woman who, in their words, had 'misbehaved' by fleeing to Baidoa."

a421.speaker: Said Abdi Hassan Abdi, senior medical staff member with Save the Children
a421.speech: "We have learned to serve the community, and if we don't step up during difficult times like this, our education means nothing."

a421.speaker: Binyam Gebru, deputy country director for Save the Children in Somalia
a421.speech: On diversifying donors: "We are reaching out to Middle Eastern donors, to China, because there is a lesson to be learned." ; "We have been dependent on a single source for too long, and now we are looking at diversifying where our support comes from. At the end of all this, we will have to reassess the entire landscape, and I believe it will change the industry forever."

a487.speaker: Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, Somali Foreign Minister, and Sameh Shoukry, Egyptian Foreign Minister
a487.speech: Held talks in Cairo on Wednesday, discussing regional security, migration, and bilateral ties, but announced no formal agreements following the meeting; both sides reiterated support for Somalia's sovereignty and unity and stressed the need for closer coordination on shared security concerns, including the African Union Stabilization Support Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM).

a487.speaker: Ahmed Moallim Fiqi, Somali Foreign Minister
a487.speech: Appreciated Egypt's historical support in education, security training, and development assistance.

a487.speaker: Sameh Shoukry, Egyptian Foreign Minister
a487.speech: Reaffirmed Egypt's backing for Somalia's federal institutions and emphasized the importance of regional solidarity in addressing cross-border challenges.

a550.speaker: Yacoubou Malêhossou, Beninese deputy (Honourable)
a550.speech: Refused to follow Kindjanhoundé in his defection, finding the enterprise unhealthy, stating on a local radio station that he is a religious preacher and that, as such, he cannot betray.

a800.speaker: Thierno Bocar Tall, CEO of the African Company for Biofuels and Renewable Energies (SABER)
a800.speech: Gave an update on renewable energy initiatives and new projects being considered: said phase 1 of the Programme for the Development of Renewable Energies and Energy Efficiency (PRODERE I) enabled Benin to be equipped with solar power plants, 1,300 low-consumption street lamps and solar kits, that a new initiative called the Solar Energy Development Programme (PROVES) is being implemented, and announced that American and Algerian funding will support this vast undertaking in order to raise Benin's renewable energy capacity to 4,000 or even 5,000 kW.

a800.speaker: Claude Gbèdonougbo Gbaguidi, president of the Energy Regulatory Authority (ARE)
a800.speech: Gave an update on a mission commissioned by the Head of State concerning the Nangbeto dam, temporarily shut down because of work on the Athiémé bridge, reporting that the company SOGEA SATOM, with the support of the military engineering corps, is working so that by 15 June the bridge will no longer be an obstacle to the proper functioning of the dam, which supplies Benin and Togo with a total capacity of 40 MW.

a800.speaker: Camille Kpogbémabou, managing director of the Beninese Electricity Company (SBEE)
a800.speech: Gave an update on the deployment of prepaid meters in the public administration, confiding that 85% of state structures are already covered by the operation begun last August, while giving assurances about corrective measures taken; he continued that a vast project to switch the 500,000 conventional connections to prepayment is under way, and that 45,000 prepaid meters are already available while awaiting the 100,000 expected under the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA).

a800.speaker: Géro Amoussouga, interim Minister in charge of Energy, and Alassani Tigri, Secretary General of the government
a800.speech: Reassure the population as to the arrangements made to eradicate and durably avert the energy crisis in Benin.

a800.speaker: Félix Comlan Ebo
a800.speech: According to him, this is the first phase with 650 solar street lamps and six mini power plants; the second phase, financed by the Americans, will soon be implemented for 1,500 street lamps.

a877.speaker: Comfort Addai Fofie, staff midwife, Jadema Health Centre, Northeast Region
a877.speech: “Zipline’s support in delivering essential medical supplies, including their recent delivery of some much-needed drugs to our facility, has been incredibly helpful in enabling us to discharge our duties effectively. Their timely deliveries and excellent collaboration have made a significant impact on our work. We’re truly grateful to the team for their continued efforts, they mean a lot to us in our line of duty.”

a877.speaker: Daniel Kwaku Merki, Head of Zipline Ghana
a877.speech: “Ghana’s proactive approach to mobilising domestic resources and embracing innovative delivery solutions exemplifies its commitment to building a robust health system. This continued collaboration with Zipline is a clear example of how Ghana is transforming a challenging situation into an opportunity to build a more self-reliant and cost-effective health system – one that ensures critical care reaches every corner of the nation.”

a884.speaker: Office of Presidential Personnel (email)
a884.speech: Informed Paul Martin that his position was terminated “effective immediately.”

a884.speaker: USAID Office of Inspector General (report)
a884.speech: Warned that more than $489 million worth of food assistance was at risk of spoilage after the Trump administration issued an unclear aid freeze guidance, ordered staff to refrain from “external communications” and placed more than 90 percent of USAID workforce on paid administrative leave ; “According to USAID staff, this uncertainty put more than $489 million of food assistance at ports, in transit, and in warehouses at risk of spoilage, unanticipated storage needs, and diversion.”

a884.speaker: USAID Office of Inspector General
a884.speech: Said that while initial guidance provided a funding waiver for emergency food assistance, shipments were delayed globally because staff faced conflicting instructions and were concerned about breaking the order on external communications.

a884.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency
a884.speech: Asserted that USAID was “radical” and a “criminal organization.”

a884.speaker: Associated Press
a884.speech: According to the Associated Press, the U.S. is the world’s largest humanitarian donor despite spending less than 1 percent of its budget on foreign assistance.

a884.speaker: Lawmakers
a884.speech: Have lambasted the Trump administration’s decision to dismantle the agency, claiming that may only be done by an act of Congress.

a884.speaker: Organizations that represent USAID workers, companies that contract with USAID, and non-profits (lawsuits)
a884.speech: Have filed lawsuits against the Trump administration, asserting that it does not have the authority to axe the funding that was expressly provided by Congress.

a906.speaker: Al Shabaab
a906.speech: Confirmed on Saturday that leader Ahmed Abdi Godane had been killed in a US drone strike earlier last week.

a906.speaker: US spokesperson
a906.speech: Said it was a “major symbolic and operational loss” for the Somali militant group.

a906.speaker: Somalia’s national security minister
a906.speech: Was blunter, describing it as “a delightful victory”.

a906.speaker: Hassan Sheikh Mahamud, President of Somalia
a906.speech: “While an extreme hardcore may fight over the leadership of Al-Shabaab, this is a chance for the majority of members to change course and reject Godane’s decision to make them the pawns of an international terror campaign” ; he added that he was “willing to offer amnesty to Al-Shabaab members who reject violence and renounce their links to Al-Shabaab and Al-Qaeda – but for the next 45 days only.”

a906.speaker: Al Shabaab (statement)
a906.speech: Immediately named a new leader, the little known Ahmad Umar, in what it claimed was a unanimous decision; also reaffirmed its commitment to Al Qaeda, and vowed revenge: “By the permission of Allah, you will surely taste the bitter consequences of your actions”, it warned in a statement directed at the Somali government, regional armies in Somalia and the Americans with their deadly drones.

a906.speaker: Human Rights Watch (report)
a906.speech: Released a report into sexual abuse and sexual exploitation committed by Amisom soldiers against Somali women at Amisom bases in Mogadishu; the report details ten instances of sexual assault and 14 instances of sexual exploitation, but warns that this is just the tip of what could prove to be a very damaging iceberg ; “Members of African Union forces, making use of Somali intermediaries, have employed a range of tactics to get private access to Somali women and then abuse them. Some Amisom soldiers have used humanitarian assistance, provided by the mission, to coerce vulnerable women and girls into sexual activity. A number of the women and girls interviewed for this report said that they were initially approached for sex in return for money or raped while seeking medical assistance and water on the Amisom bases, particularly the Burundian contingent’s base. Others were enticed directly from internally displaced persons (IDP) camps to start working on the Amisom base camp by female friends and neighbors, some of whom were already working on the base. Some of the women who were raped said that the soldiers gave them food or money afterwards in an apparent attempt to frame the assault as transactional sex or discourage them from filing a complaint or seeking redress.”

a906.speaker: Women and girls interviewed for the Human Rights Watch report
a906.speech: Said that they were initially approached for sex in return for money or raped while seeking medical assistance and water on the Amisom bases, particularly the Burundian contingent’s base; some of the women who were raped said that the soldiers gave them food or money afterwards.

a906.speaker: Sheik Abdul Asis Abu Muscab, Al Shabaab military spokesman (photo caption)
a906.speech: Issues a statement south of capital Mogadishu October 19, 2011.

a1049.speaker: A witness in Port Sudan (anonymous)
a1049.speech: Said explosions and fires rocked Sudan's main port city and wartime capital Port Sudan on Tuesday, part of a days-long drone assault, and that blasts had been heard from other areas though it was not clear exactly where else had been hit.

a1049.speaker: Reuters (video and @Reuters social media post, 6 May 2025)
a1049.speech: A Reuters video showed a massive column of black smoke billowing from the area around the port; the Reuters post stated: "Explosions and fires rocked Sudan's wartime capital Port Sudan, a witness said, part of a days-long drone assault that has torched the country's biggest fuel depots and damaged its primary gateway for humanitarian aid in a major escalation."

a1049.speaker: Sudan's electricity company
a1049.speech: Said a substation in the city was also hit, causing a complete power outage, part of a systematic assault on infrastructure.

a1049.speaker: Military sources (anonymous)
a1049.speech: Have blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) for the attacks on Port Sudan since Sunday.

a1049.speaker: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
a1049.speech: Has not yet claimed any responsibility for the strikes.

a1049.speaker: Witnesses (anonymous)
a1049.speech: Said one of the targets was a major hotel near the residence of Sudan's military leader, General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.

a1049.speaker: A military source (anonymous)
a1049.speech: Said the army had destroyed an aircraft and weapons depots in the RSF-controlled Nyala airport in Darfur, the main stronghold of the paramilitary group.

a1049.speaker: Egypt and Saudi Arabia
a1049.speech: The attacks have drawn condemnation from neighbouring Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

a1049.speaker: United Nations
a1049.speech: Expressed concern over the attacks; the UN has called the situation in Sudan the world's biggest humanitarian disaster.

a1049.speaker: Sudan's army-aligned government
a1049.speech: Has accused the United Arab Emirates of backing the RSF, and accused the UAE of fuelling genocide in a case at the International Court of Justice.

a1049.speaker: UN experts
a1049.speech: Have found the accusations that the United Arab Emirates is backing the RSF credible.

a1049.speaker: International Court of Justice
a1049.speech: Said on Monday it could not rule in a case in which the Sudanese government accused the UAE of fuelling genocide.

a1049.speaker: United Nations
a1049.speech: According to the UN, the war, triggered by a dispute over a transition to civilian rule, has displaced over 12 million people and pushed half the population into acute hunger.

a1051.speaker: British High Commission (published statement)
a1051.speech: Indicates that the reforms include simplified rules of origin that will enable Malawian exporters to source inputs for finished goods from across the continent while maintaining tariff-free access to the UK market; it says the change is expected to support not only UK-Africa trade but also intra-African commerce, helping to unlock the African Continental Free Trade Area's estimated $3.4 trillion potential.

a1051.speaker: Jenny Chapman, UK Minister for Development
a1051.speech: Is quoted as saying the shift in the UK's approach to developing country partnerships would be mutually beneficial: "These new rules will make it easier for developing countries to trade more closely with the UK. This is good for their economies and for UK consumers and businesses."

a1051.speaker: Statistics on UK imports from Africa (UK development trading arrangements data)
a1051.speech: Show that over 3.2 billion pounds worth of goods imported into the UK from African countries benefited from preferences granted by the UK's development trading arrangements last year.

a1051.speaker: Douglas Alexander, UK Minister for Trade Policy
a1051.speech: Highlighted the importance of trade in poverty reduction, noting that: "No country has ever lifted itself out of poverty without trading with its neighbours." ; He added that trade has been "an essential ingredient in lifting hundreds of millions of people out of poverty around the globe" over recent decades.

a1051.speaker: Vitumbiko Mumba, Malawi Minister of Industry and Trade
a1051.speech: Said in a recent interview that Malawi's economic development could be enhanced through sound trade relations with other nations.

a1132.speaker: Several petitioners before the Fourth Committee of the UN General Assembly
a1132.speech: Denounced the serious and persistent human rights violations in the Tindouf camps in south-western Algeria, where children are reportedly forcibly recruited by the armed militias of the Polisario Front ; The petitioners unanimously called for an independent international investigation and for effective protection of the fundamental rights of children and civilians in these camps, administered, according to them, "with the complicity of the host country, Algeria".

a1132.speaker: Amanda DiCianni, representative of the NGO Rescue and Relief International
a1132.speech: Stated that "the international community has been sounding the alarm for years about the recruitment and militarization of children by the Polisario in the Tindouf camps." According to her, these facts "are not mere allegations, but documented observations" already mentioned within the UN and confirmed by the Human Rights Council in Geneva ; She denounced "the lack of transparency and security in these camps controlled by armed militias", citing "corruption on an industrial scale" and "proven links between certain leaders of the separatist movement and transnational criminal networks".

a1132.speaker: Erragheb Hormatallah, president of the municipal council of Dakhla
a1132.speech: Called on the international community to "remind the Polisario leaders that international law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child apply to everyone, including the host country of these camps".

a1132.speaker: Laila El Atfani, of the NGO Refai
a1132.speech: Denounced "the systematic indoctrination of children torn from school and trained in military camps", seeing in it a "real threat to regional peace and stability". She stressed that "the autonomy plan presented by Morocco in 2007 remains the only realistic basis for guaranteeing the dignity and protection of the sequestered populations".

a1132.speaker: Grace Njapau, former Zambian Minister of the Interior, and Wilson Lalengke, Indonesian journalist, among other speakers
a1132.speech: Spoke of "extrajudicial executions, massive diversions of humanitarian aid and a climate of terror imposed by the separatist militias".

a1132.speaker: Nancy Huff, American president of Teach the Children International
a1132.speech: Described the Tindouf camps as a "breeding ground for extremism, radicalization and trafficking of all kinds", considering that "the Moroccan autonomy plan, supported by several world powers, represents the most pragmatic solution for development and regional stability".

a1155.speaker: Citizen's Observatory for Health (Mozambican NGO)
a1155.speech: Said on Thursday that Mozambique should think about strategies to reduce external dependence in the face of the cut in US international aid, considering that the measure has an "enormous impact" on the country.

a1155.speaker: Jorge Matine, director of the Citizen's Observatory for Health
a1155.speech: "As a country, we always have to think about how to reduce external dependence and how to improve cooperation because there are issues that Mozambique won't be able to solve on its own; it needs the learning and support of other countries." ; Said more than 70% of Mozambique's public health system for the areas of HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, family planning and laboratories depends on funds from donors, including the US government, so the suspension of funding has a "huge and significant impact" on the country's health services ; "It's a significant impact, there will be a paralysis of services (…) In less than three to six months, it's very difficult for the government to mobilise enough resources to replace American funds, which will not be possible." ; Defended the need for the Mozambican government to negotiate an "acceptable timeframe" with the US and other donors, between one and two years, to "gradually start thinking" about internal strategies for reorganising the financing of health services, warning of future "shocks" ; "We need to be able to learn that, as well as shocks from pandemics, we will have shocks like these from governments that we have no control over (…). So [we need to] better coordinate aid so that it is aid that does not create high dependency, but at the same time how to take advantage of cooperation to strengthen our national health system."

a1155.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State and new acting director of USAID
a1155.speech: Accused USAID of being "completely lacking in response capacity", criticising the "insubordination" in that body.

a1155.speaker: Donald Trump, US President; Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE); and some Republican congressmen
a1155.speech: Have criticised USAID—which oversees humanitarian, development, and security programmes in around 120 countries—in increasingly harsh terms, accusing it of promoting progressive causes.

a1212.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1212.speech: Speaking at a conference in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, highlighted the urgent need for assistance, with 33 million people in the region requiring humanitarian aid, including 11 million internally displaced persons and refugees ; urged donors to fully fund the UN's response plans, which are currently only 40% funded.

a1212.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1212.speech: Emphasized the importance of addressing the root causes of the crisis, including poverty, inequality, climate change, and conflict.

a1212.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1212.speech: Stressed the potential of the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin regions, with their young populations and abundant natural resources.

a1212.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1212.speech: Called for a comprehensive approach that includes humanitarian aid, development assistance, and peacebuilding efforts. He emphasized the need to protect civilians, ensure unhindered humanitarian access, and promote dialogue and reconciliation.

a1261.speaker: Namibia's Permanent Representative to the United Nations
a1261.speech: Has called for stronger international support to improve access to affordable HIV medicines and ensure sustainable funding for HIV programmes around the world.

a1261.speaker: Johanna Haimene, Oshana Health Director
a1261.speech: Said the region has recorded significant progress in the number of people accessing HIV treatment, whose number currently stands at over 20,000.

a1261.speaker: Dr. Esperance Luvindao, Namibian Minister of Health and Social Services
a1261.speech: Has announced that Namibia will move towards regulatory approval for the rollout of Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection for the treatment and prevention of HIV.

a1261.speaker: Sustjie Mbumba, First Lady of Namibia
a1261.speech: During the opening of a high-level Roundtable Discussion on inequalities, HIV, TB, Malaria, and Pandemics at State House, Madame Mbumba encouraged individuals and organisations to speak out against inequality or injustice.

a1261.speaker: New health director of the Kavango East Region (unnamed)
a1261.speech: Urged the community to offer love and support to the affected and infected, following high HIV infection and transmission in the Kavango East Region.

a1261.speaker: Executive Director, Ministry of Health and Social Services (MoHSS) of Namibia
a1261.speech: Said HIV prevalence among pregnant women has declined from 22% in 2002 to 14% last year, while welcoming the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator, Ambassador Dr. John Nkengasong, on a visit to the Katutura State Hospital.

a1261.speaker: Ambassador John Nkengasong, US Global AIDS Coordinator
a1261.speech: Says PEPFAR has invested over N$27 billion in Namibia over the past 18 years.

a1261.speaker: Nicholus Mutenda, Health Control Programme Officer, Directorate of Special Programmes, Ministry of Health and Social Services
a1261.speech: Says Namibia is doing well in terms of HIV Strategic response.

a1402.speaker: United Nations and World Food Programme (WFP)
a1402.speech: According to the United Nations and the World Food Programme, the humanitarian situation in the Democratic Republic of Congo is reaching a critical level; in Goma, a strategic city for humanitarian aid, basic services are paralysed, threatening millions of people displaced by the conflict.

a1402.speaker: United Nations
a1402.speech: Is also worried about the situation in South Kivu, where the M23 is advancing rapidly toward the city of Bukavu, further aggravating the crisis. Faced with this dramatic situation, the UN is calling for urgent intervention to secure the delivery of humanitarian aid and protect civilian populations.

a1402.speaker: Shelley Thakral, spokesperson for the World Food Programme (WFP)
a1402.speech: Warns of critical shortages and describes a dramatic situation: "People cruelly lack food, drinking water, medical supplies and that is very worrying. The supply chain is no longer assured at the moment, because everything is closed, whether road access or air access. Our first priority is of course the safety of staff. We will resume our activities as soon as security allows us to."

a1661.speaker: The Journal of African Business (September/October/November 2025 issue)
a1661.speech: Outlines key continental initiatives with implications for Eswatini's private sector, from trade reforms to infrastructure and water partnerships, signalling new opportunities and challenges for local enterprises. Notes that regional partnerships are becoming critical as climate variability, ageing infrastructure and urbanisation increase pressure on water resources. Emphasises the growing role of the African Private Sector Hearings (APSH) in shaping trade policy under the AfCFTA framework, and points to rising opportunities in renewable energy and environmental, social and governance (ESG) compliance across Africa.

a1661.speaker: Magalies Water (South African water utility)
a1661.speech: Revealed that its Scientific Services Division has conducted benchmarking sessions with the Eswatini Water Services Corporation (EWSC) as part of a regional effort to strengthen laboratory services and water quality management standards across the Southern African Development Community (SADC).

a1661.speaker: Industry experts
a1661.speech: Argue that ESG compliance is becoming a key requirement for accessing international financing and export markets, meaning Eswatini's businesses will need to align with these standards to stay competitive.

a1694.speaker: Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry of Ghana
a1694.speech: Urged the board to provide strategic oversight to strengthen quality assurance systems and consumer safety in the country's markets, and charged it to drive the harmonisation of standards in support of Ghana's participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA): "We also want you to work very hard in the area of the African Continental Free Trade Area because it is our best bet. We need to do a lot of standard harmonisation because once we harmonise our standards with other countries, it makes trading with those countries very easy under the African Continental Free Trade Area," she emphasised.

a1694.speaker: Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry of Ghana
a1694.speech: Reiterated the importance of the GSA's role in facilitating trade, protecting consumers, and improving the competitiveness of Ghanaian products in international markets.

a1694.speaker: Hudu Mogtari, Chairperson of the Ghana Standards Authority board
a1694.speech: Pledged the board's commitment to collaborate with GSA's management and staff in executing its mandate effectively: "I wish to commit that we will work together to enhance the work of the Ghana Standards Authority, working with management and staff of Ghana Standards Authority. We believe that the job of protecting the safety of consumers, protecting industry and contributing to the development of this country is our key priority and we must make sure that we work towards that," he said.

a1758.speaker: Moody's Investors Service (credit rating report)
a1758.speech: Further downgraded Ethiopia's creditworthiness from Caa1 to Caa2, citing delays and ambiguity in debt reprofiling, economic volatility and political instability in the country. "No tangible developments have occurred other than the formation of a creditors committee," reads the report. Decisions on what the debt treatment will involve are pending, and there is fear this would take time for Ethiopia to access official and market-based loans; liquidity risks have heightened, and associated default risks have increased to levels Moody's finds more consistent with a Caa2 rating.

a1758.speaker: Moody's Investors Service (credit rating report)
a1758.speech: Blames growing political uncertainty, threats of sanctions and suspension of development assistance for defaulting. The report says the political tension is unlikely to be resolved in the foreseeable future and has heightened these risks. "Such deep tensions and conflict are likely weighing on some creditors' ability and readiness to provide financing or debt relief, further contributing to default risk." The report also claims the longer official creditors take to begin talks and agree on a debt treatment, the higher the risk for private-sector creditors involved.

a1758.speaker: Ministry of Finance of Ethiopia
a1758.speech: Last month announced the formation of a creditors committee chaired by France and China.

a1758.speaker: A macroeconomist (anonymous, spoke to Fortune on condition of anonymity)
a1758.speech: Said that lack of clarity on the outstanding stock of Chinese debt to Ethiopia has become a stumbling block to move forward in the negotiations. "Unless that's resolved, the common framework won't make any progress."

a1758.speaker: Alisa Strobel, senior economist for Sub-Saharan Africa at IHS Markit
a1758.speech: Concurs, saying that a lack of transparency over the debt owed to Chinese lenders, such as loans granted to state-owned enterprises, is often an issue for private creditors; debt restructuring from major non-commercial lenders should ideally be completed first.

a1758.speaker: Alisa Strobel, senior economist for Sub-Saharan Africa at IHS Markit
a1758.speech: "There is certainly an element of heightened political instability that comes into play on why we see delays in the restructuring of the country's official sovereign debt."

a1758.speaker: Alisa Strobel, senior economist for Sub-Saharan Africa at IHS Markit
a1758.speech: Is under the impression that the involvement of private creditors would be unlikely or minor at best. "We also have to keep in mind that the bulk of Ethiopia's public external debt is official multilateral and bilateral debt."

a1758.speaker: Alisa Strobel, senior economist for Sub-Saharan Africa at IHS Markit
a1758.speech: Says a two-step approach is needed: resolving the war in the northern part positively signals the international community and speeds up the Common Framework process; cautions that the lack of progress in entering new facilities with the IMF would likely hinder Ethiopia's efforts to renegotiate its international debt under the G20 common framework. "Improving international relations and restoring Ethiopia's reputation is key. Ethiopian authorities have shown a willingness to work with the IMF in the recent past."

a1758.speaker: Eyob Tekalign (PhD), State Minister for Finance of Ethiopia
a1758.speech: Says in his media briefings last month that public creditors would identify parameters for equal treatment, a consideration in a debt-restructuring agreement with the Paris Club creditors that the debtor should secure at least comparable relief from other creditors.

a1898.speaker: Government of Ethiopia
a1898.speech: Announced this weekend the relocation of 80,000 residents to other places following at least ten earthquakes reported in the Ethiopian Rift Valley over the past month.

a1898.speaker: United States Geological Survey
a1898.speech: Recorded last Saturday the largest earthquake, with a magnitude of 5.8, about 56 kilometres south-east of Ambosa, in the Oromia region, in the early hours of Saturday.

a1898.speaker: Atalay Ayele, head of the seismology department and professor of seismic science at Addis Ababa University
a1898.speech: Said the epicentre was in the middle of Mount Dofen, in the Awash Fentale district, in the Afar region.

a1898.speaker: Ahmed Ibrahim, coordinator of the zone's command post
a1898.speech: Confirming the relocation of the herders, said that humanitarian aid was being provided to the people affected by the relocation process.

a1898.speaker: Binyam Wubshat, representative of the Kesem dam administration
a1898.speech: "The Kesem dam, built to mitigate land erosion, is designed to withstand earthquakes of a magnitude of up to seven on the Richter scale," ; "No problem linked to land displacement has been reported so far," he added.

a1898.speaker: Recent reports (unattributed)
a1898.speech: Indicate that the Kesem sugar factory, located in the Dulasa district in the Afar region, has suffered significant damage due to the ongoing earthquakes.

a1898.speaker: Government of Ethiopia (statement)
a1898.speech: "The government is closely following events with experts on the ground. In addition, it has identified the epicentre of the earthquake and deployed rescuers from various fields in 12 localities to assess the extent of the damage," the Ethiopian government said in a statement.

a1960.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Tanzanian Minister of Finance
a1960.speech: Presented the draft budget for the 2025/26 financial year to Parliament on June 12, 2025, outlining the government's projected revenue and expenditure. According to the Minister, one of the key assumptions guiding the budget is the need to strengthen resilience to disasters such as droughts and floods.

a1960.speaker: 2025/26 budget speech / draft budget (Government of Tanzania document)
a1960.speech: Identifies climate change as a potential risk to its successful implementation and reiterates the importance of continuing to address climate risks through the implementation of existing strategies, including the National Environmental Master Plan for Strategic Interventions (2022-2032) and the National Cooking Strategy (2024-2034).

a1960.speaker: National Environmental Master Plan for Strategic Interventions (2022-2032) (policy document)
a1960.speech: Stresses the need to reduce emissions from transportation and industrial activities.

a1960.speaker: Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) of Tanzania (document)
a1960.speech: Sets targets of reducing greenhouse gas emissions economy-wide between 30-35 per cent by 2030 and identifies energy as a top priority for transitioning to a low-emission economy.

a2128.speaker: Beauty Narteh, Ghana's Anti-Corruption Coalition
a2128.speech: Said her group wanted a fairer tax system and "dignity, not handouts."

a2128.speaker: Sokhna Ndiaye, Africa Development Interchange Network
a2128.speech: Called on the public and private sectors to be "less selfish and show more solidarity" with developing countries.

a2128.speaker: Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister
a2128.speech: Said that "the very fact that this conference is happening while conflict is raging across the globe is a reason to be hopeful". ; Speaking at an event by non-profit Global Citizen, Sanchez reiterated Madrid's commitment to reach 0.7% of GDP in development aid and urged other countries to do the same.

a2128.speaker: Jason Braganza, executive director of pan-African advocacy group AFRODAD
a2128.speech: Said countries including the U.S., the European Union and Britain had obstructed efforts to organise a UN convention on sovereign debt. ; "It's a shame these countries have opted to protect their own interests and those of creditors over lives that are being lost."

a2291.speaker: Mozambican government
a2291.speech: In April this year, the Mozambican government disclosed previously hidden, government-guaranteed loans exceeding $1-billion (possibly as much as $1.4-billion) to state defence and security companies.

a2291.speaker: Mozambican government
a2291.speech: has just announced that the 24 ships will have to be re-fitted in South Africa to meet European Union (EU) specifications so it can export tuna to the EU.

a2291.speaker: Some analysts
a2291.speech: believe this debt could rise to around US$2.35 billion with further revelations.

a2291.speaker: Analysts
a2291.speech: say a large chunk of the Ematum loan was diverted into security agencies.

a2291.speaker: Opposition parties (Mozambique)
a2291.speech: have called for [former President Armando] Guebuza's arrest.

a2291.speaker: Bloomberg
a2291.speech: reported last week that the international gas exploration companies Eni and Anadarko, which are among the biggest potential investors in Mozambique's huge gas reserves, were reconsidering their investments in light of the expanding debt crisis.

a2291.speaker: Chris Bredenhann, partner at PricewaterhouseCoopers in Cape Town
a2291.speech: "The uncertainty in the country does create a challenge on the way forward." ; "The project is pivotal for the development and growth of Mozambique."

a2291.speaker: Sasol (South Africa)
a2291.speech: said it was forging ahead with its plans to spend $1.4-billion on tapping its Temane and Pande gas fields in northern Mozambique; and pumping the gas through its 865km pipeline to South Africa's power-starved commercial hub, Gauteng.

a2291.speaker: Christine Lagarde, IMF Managing Director
a2291.speech: told the BBC last month that, by hiding the loans, the Mozambique government was "clearly concealing corruption".

a2291.speaker: Renamo (the Mozambican National Resistance)
a2291.speech: its casus belli, that the Frelimo government is not serving the people's interests and should be removed - by whatever means.

a2291.speaker: Andre Thomashausen, University of South Africa law professor and Mozambique expert
a2291.speech: "The loans - at unusually high interest rates of 12% - have bankrupted the fifth most underdeveloped nation globally, according to United Nations Development Programme data." ; "With less than half the loan amounts, Mozambique could have easily funded the economic and social developments and reintegration measures needed to turn the country away from the very imminent danger of a renewed civil war."

a2378.speaker: Jeune Afrique (French edition)
a2378.speech: Reported that during a meeting between the head of the United States Africa Command and Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, the parties agreed to create a forward base in Côte d'Ivoire to receive the American contingent from Niger.

a2378.speaker: Local experts
a2378.speech: According to local experts, Mauritania could be one of the countries where the Pentagon seeks to establish itself in the Sahel.

a2534.speaker: Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch
a2534.speech: The sanctions "will prevent victims from having access to justice."

a2534.speaker: Washington (US government)
a2534.speech: Washington faults the International Criminal Court over the arrest warrants issued in November against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant.

a2534.speaker: International Criminal Court (ICC)
a2534.speech: The ICC laments that the American sanctions hamper work on a wide range of investigations, and not only the one concerning the Israeli leaders ; The ICC suspects the two Israelis of war crimes, for restricting humanitarian aid and intentionally targeting civilians in the military operation against Hamas in Gaza.

a2534.speaker: Tel Aviv (Israeli government)
a2534.speech: Tel Aviv has always disputed this.

a2803.speaker: Mohamed Ali Nafti, Tunisian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Migration and Tunisians Abroad, and Badr Abdelatty, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2803.speech: reaffirmed the need for close coordination among Arab and Muslim countries ; argued for collective diplomatic action in order to anticipate security risks and promote lasting political solutions ; highlighted the strength of bilateral ties between Tunisia and Egypt, calling for stronger cooperation in several sectors of common interest, and agreed to continue consultations ahead of the next bilateral meetings planned in the coming weeks.

a2803.speaker: Badr Abdelatty, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a2803.speech: recalled the efforts under way in Cairo to reach a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, as well as to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.

a2803.speaker: Coordination of the Al Soumoud humanitarian caravan
a2803.speech: announced its return to Tunisia on Monday, after being refused permission to pass by the Egyptian and Libyan authorities.

a3206.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a3206.speech: In a media briefing on Tuesday, highlighted the consequences of funding suspensions, including disruptions to HIV treatment, setbacks in polio eradication and limited resources for responding to mpox epidemics in Africa ; “The suspension of funding to PEPFAR, the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, caused an immediate stop to HIV treatment, testing and prevention services in the 50 countries” ; noted that despite a waiver for life-saving services, prevention programmes for at-risk groups remain excluded, clinics have closed, and health workers have been put on leave ; urged the US Government to reconsider its funding approach, at least until alternative solutions can be found to maintain essential health services.

a3206.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a3206.speech: Provided updates on the recently reported Ebola outbreak in Uganda, with nine confirmed cases, including one death.

a3206.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a3206.speech: “At most, only one-third of people who need health services in North and South Kivu are able to receive them,” Tedros stated, emphasising the risks posed by infectious disease outbreaks such as mpox and cholera.

a3206.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a3206.speech: “Yesterday, we began distributing childhood cancer medicines at no cost in the first two countries: Mongolia and Uzbekistan,” said Tedros, adding that shipments are planned for four more countries.

a3206.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a3206.speech: Announced progress in expanding access to childhood cancer medicines in low and middle-income countries.

a3206.speaker: UN News
a3206.speech: Reported on Tuesday that WHO announced progress in expanding access to childhood cancer medicines in low and middle-income countries.

a3355.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique, and Ahmed Attaf, Algerian Minister of Foreign Affairs
a3355.speech: Reaffirmed, during the audience, the commitment of Mozambique and Algeria to strengthening political, economic and social cooperation.

a3355.speaker: Ahmed Attaf, Algerian Minister of Foreign Affairs and the National Community Abroad, Special Envoy of President Abdelmadjid Tebboune
a3355.speech: Highlighted his satisfaction and the honour of being in Mozambique, a country which, according to him, occupies a special place in the hearts of the Algerian people, and recalled the importance of historic Mozambican figures such as Eduardo Mondlane, Samora Machel and Joaquim Chissano, considered true heroes of African liberation: "Mozambique is the birthplace of great leaders who inspired the struggle for independence across the continent. Eduardo Mondlane, Samora Machel and Joaquim Chissano are names that continue to echo in Algeria as symbols of courage and determination in the quest for freedom and for the development of Africa." ; Stressed that the friendship between Mozambique and Algeria has deep roots, established during the colonial period, when the two countries mutually supported each other's liberation struggles.

a3355.speaker: Ahmed Attaf, Algerian Minister of Foreign Affairs and the National Community Abroad, Special Envoy of President Abdelmadjid Tebboune
a3355.speech: Explained that his mission in Mozambique had three main objectives: to express Algeria's appreciation for Mozambican support in the African Union elections; to highlight the effective collaboration between the two countries on the United Nations Security Council; and he underlined Mozambique's commitment to the African Union, contributing to the stability and development of the continent.

a3355.speaker: Ahmed Attaf, Algerian Minister of Foreign Affairs and the National Community Abroad, Special Envoy of President Abdelmadjid Tebboune
a3355.speech: Praised the progress in bilateral relations, highlighting cooperation in various strategic areas, and emphasised that both countries share common values of solidarity, peace and development, which has been essential to strengthening dialogue and concertation on international issues ; Said that Algeria and Mozambique share a common vision on sustainable development and on strengthening Africa's position in world geopolitics, stressing that the two countries will continue to work together to ensure that their aspirations are met within international organisations ; Assured that Algeria is willing to expand cooperation with Mozambique in strategic areas such as trade, education, health and security, and stressed that, beyond political diplomacy, there is strong interest in strengthening economic and social partnerships, creating opportunities for investment and joint development ; "The message was very substantial and there were promises of a bright outlook in relations between Mozambique and Algeria. The basis of this partnership is the values we share: justice, freedom and cooperation, always with the vision of guaranteeing Africa the place it deserves in the international community."

a3358.speaker: Women for Peace Envoy South Sudan (WPESS) (statement shared with Eye Radio)
a3358.speech: Announced the successful hosting of the "Sport for Peace" event on 15th-16th March: "To foster trust, dialogue, and peaceful coexistence among communities affected by conflict, the tournament united six Bomas — Labato, Lowudo, Alia, Lerwa, Cama, and Licari — engaging 325 players (150 women, 150 men and 25 community leaders) and drawing over 1,000 spectators." ; "A key focus of the event was to encourage women's participation in sports, creating a supportive environment where they felt safe, motivated, and empowered to take part."

a3358.speaker: Participants in the tournament
a3358.speech: Said that they enjoyed the fun atmosphere and highlighted how important it is to create opportunities where diverse communities are united.

a3358.speaker: Community members of Obbo Payam
a3358.speech: Made a collective commitment to take an active role in peacebuilding, engaging in conflict resolution efforts within their villages, Bomas, and broader communities.

a3379.speaker: G7 official (anonymous), in a closed-door speech on trade and finance
a3379.speech: “Europe’s new external investment strategy must reconnect with historical commercial models. We are returning to the white elephants of the 1970s, because that is what our partners want.” — describing the EU’s interest in financing heavy infrastructure with the promise of investment and growth for recipient countries.

a3379.speaker: Josep Borrell (2024), High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy / Vice-President of the European Commission
a3379.speech: “The era of Western domination is definitively over.”

a3379.speaker: Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso (governments)
a3379.speech: On 28 January 2024 announced their withdrawal from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), a decision linked to the series of sanctions imposed by ECOWAS on their military governments and to the countries’ objection to French influence in the bloc.

a3379.speaker: Government of Niger
a3379.speech: In March 2024 suspended all its military relations with the United States, citing problems related to US encroachment on its sovereignty.

a3379.speaker: Capasso & Kadri (2023), Ajl (2024) and Yeros (2024)
a3379.speech: Have argued that the notion of imperialism is anchored in a historical structure of global capitalism, which cannot be abstracted and applied selectively to the new bipolar world.

a3379.speaker: Samir Amin (2018)
a3379.speech: “Deng Xiaoping said that one had to begin by examining the real facts. That is exactly what conventional professional ‘economists’ - all of them, including the Chinese ‘experts’ trained in the United States and brainwashed - do not do.”

a3484.speaker: Gen. Augustino Maduot, SSFA President
a3484.speech: Highlighted the importance of the training, stating that the knowledge gained could lead to financial benefits for participants ; urged them to take the course seriously and use their new skills to scout potential players for the national team.

a3484.speaker: Ali Mwebe, Football Development Director at FUFA
a3484.speech: Emphasized the importance of bilateral cooperation between South Sudan and Uganda in advancing football development ; described the initiative as "an investment in the future of South Sudanese football."

a3704.speaker: Cllr Cooper W. Kruah, Minister of Labor of Liberia
a3704.speech: Urged stakeholders in the education sector to ensure that no student should face discrimination based on gender, ethnic origin, disability, cultural background, religion, political affiliation, marital status, speaking at the launch of the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) policy of the National Commission on Higher Education: “With these policy standards, students at our tertiary institutions, are therefore expected to maximize their learning without any hindrance, whatsoever” ; “Engaging in policy development and reform is an effective means of bolstering the impact educational leaders have on those they serve” ; “We are therefore elated to know that through this policy, institutions are encouraged to prevent discrimination, enhance fairness, promote equal opportunity, and provide support services for staff, students and other educational stakeholders in our country” ; “In the continuously evolving world of education, policy, and governance are integral components of effective leadership Developing a deep understanding of policy and governance structures, including how they are created and implemented as well as how they impact learning environments and stakeholders is essential for aspiring educational leaders.”

a3704.speaker: Cllr Cooper W. Kruah, Minister of Labor of Liberia
a3704.speech: Noted that the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) policy, a collaborative initiative of the NCHE and USAID, through the TESTS project, actually aims at ensuring a gender-free and inclusive learning environment to induce the acquiring of quality learning objectives by students, and seeks to provide guidance for higher education institutions in Liberia: “The policy complements NCHE's reform initiatives to promote quality and excellence in tertiary education across universities and colleges in Liberia.”

a3704.speaker: Dr. Jarso Maley Jallah, Minister of Education of Liberia
a3704.speech: Emphasized the importance of cultivating a learning atmosphere that prioritizes diversity and inclusion, and highlighted that educational institutions should serve as dynamic communities enriched by diverse voices and perspectives, which enhance academic discourse and broaden worldviews ; noted that the policy will implement stringent measures against gender-based violence and discrimination while advocating for gender equity in hiring and leadership roles: “This initiative represents a strong commitment to inclusive education in Liberia, paving the way for a brighter and more equitable future for all learners and educators.”

a3711.speaker: Michael Kaiyatsa, Executive Director of the Centre for Human Rights and Rehabilitation
a3711.speech: Said many civil society organisations in Malawi are facing existential threats: “Many are experiencing significant budget shortfalls that could lead to staff layoffs, the suspension of outreach initiatives and a diminished capacity to monitor human rights abuses and governance failures” ; admitted: “No single donor can match the scale and scope of support previously provided by USaid.”

a3711.speaker: Habiba Osman, Executive Secretary of the Malawi Human Rights Commission
a3711.speech: Echoed similar concerns, saying that the freeze has not only affected the human rights sector but also the broader humanitarian field: “These freezes are more than just budget line adjustments; they are lifelines lost, programmes stalled and critical support withheld from vulnerable communities.”

a3711.speaker: Habiba Osman, Executive Secretary of the Malawi Human Rights Commission
a3711.speech: Believes that a national task force may be needed to address the funding gap, urging the government to take a leadership role: “All sectors need a sober reflection on what mitigating steps to take. The government must lead this conversation because most funds pass through it.”

a3711.speaker: Charles Kajoloweka, Executive Director of Youth and Society
a3711.speech: Warned that the freeze will disproportionately affect the youth, particularly in health and human rights programmes: “Most youth programmes on health and human rights were funded by USaid. This will really shrink the civic space for the players in the human rights sector. We need to see how other organisations can help the situation.”

a3711.speaker: Reports (unnamed) on voter education funding
a3711.speech: Reports indicate that Malawi faces a K30 billion deficit for voter education, potentially undermining efforts to ensure free and fair elections.

a3774.speaker: Sudan Liberation Army Movement
a3774.speech: According to the movement, the natural disaster that devastated Tarais, a mountain village in Darfur, on Sunday caused more than a thousand deaths and "completely destroyed" this isolated and hard-to-reach area.

a3774.speaker: Mamou Ali Fossou, Chairman of the African Union Commission
a3774.speech: Expressed "profound compassion" in the face of the natural tragedy; "received with profound sorrow the news of the tragic landslide that occurred on 31 August in the village of Taurina"; conveyed "his most sincere condolences to the families of the victims" and underlined his solidarity "with the sole survivor, whose resilience inspires respect and hope".

a3774.speaker: African Union (statement issued from headquarters in Addis Ababa)
a3774.speech: "In these painful circumstances, the chairman of the Commission reaffirms the unwavering solidarity of the African Union with the affected populations and calls on all Sudanese stakeholders to silence the guns and come together to facilitate the rapid and effective delivery of emergency humanitarian assistance to those who need it."

a4512.speaker: Standard & Poor's (S&P), financial rating agency
a4512.speech: Lowered its local currency rating on Mozambique to 'SD' (selective default) from 'CCC-'; writes that "Mozambique exchanged Mozambican metical (MZN) 3.7 billion ($54 million) in local currency bonds maturing in March 2025 in return for longer-dated, lower-yielding bonds maturing in March 2030," pointing out that the "ongoing recourse to such liability management operations, coupled with a history of delayed payments on domestic debt, reflects the sovereign's constrained fiscal and liquidity positions"; considers "this transaction distressed and tantamount to default" ; says Mozambique "switched the original four-year bonds maturing in March 2025, paying an annual coupon of 16.43%, for new five-year bonds with an interest rate of 14.25%," and recalls the government had "previously exchanged MZN5.7 billion ($89 million) four-year bonds maturing in October 2024 for five-year bonds due in October 2029"; says investor participation fell from 90% in the first exchange to 71% this month and that "the government is planning additional debt switches in May and September this year, alongside some in 2026"; states that "the government's ongoing and planned recourse to debt switches at such low rating levels signals its constrained capacity to manage sizeable upcoming debt maturities amid tight liquidity."

a4512.speaker: Standard & Poor's (S&P) analysts
a4512.speech: Say "Local currency debt redemptions will rise to MZN38.4 billion (2.4% of GDP) in 2025 and MZN37.1 billion (2.1% of GDP) in 2026, from 1.2% of GDP in 2024"; that these "higher local currency debt payments could increase risks of delayed payments or prompt a broader restructuring of domestic debt", in a context where the "local financial sector is already highly exposed to the sovereign, with over 20% of total banking system assets in government securities"; write that "foreign currency debt repayments will remain reasonably modest until Mozambique's sole Eurobond starts amortizing from 2028" and add that "Despite tight liquidity conditions, the government continues to service the coupon on its 2031 Eurobond; this stands at 9% ($81 million per year) until 2028 and will decrease thereafter as the outstanding amount of the bond reduces through principal amortization"; say "Amortization will be $225 million annually for 2028-2031 before production at the mega gas projects starts, anticipated in 2030", concluding that "positively, US Exim Bank re-approved a $4.7 billion loan to TotalEnergies SE in March 2025 that had been a key impediment to lifting force majeure on the project".

a4512.speaker: Standard & Poor's (S&P) on foreign currency debt
a4512.speech: Says it is maintaining the foreign currency rating, not least because commercial debt repayments 'remain modest', but warns that "potential delays to gas projects and foreign aid flows, alongside an uncertain external financing outlook, add to the pressures on Mozambique's finances".

a4717.speaker: Imali Hermann Djetta, President of the National Chamber of Agriculture of Benin
